label: Differential Equations Behind Flows
notes: Appendix D, printed pages 663 through 683, collects the ordinary differential equation facts that make the theory of flows work. Everything later about integral curves and one-parameter groups of diffeomorphisms rests on the existence, uniqueness, and smooth-dependence theorems we review here in coordinates.

label: First-Order Systems and the IVP
notes: A vector field in a chart becomes a first-order system. We fix notation: the unknown is a curve, the data is a right-hand side and a starting point, and an integral curve is one whose velocity matches the field at every instant. Higher-order equations reduce to this form.

label: Integral Curves of a Vector Field
notes: The slope field picture is the right intuition. Through each point passes exactly one trajectory tangent to the arrows. I want students to read the existence and uniqueness theorem geometrically first: distinct integral curves never cross, because crossing would give two solutions through one point.

label: The Integral Equation
notes: Integrating the system converts the initial value problem into an equivalent integral equation. This is the pivotal move: a continuous solution of the integral equation is automatically differentiable and solves the original system. It also packages the initial condition directly into the equation, which is exactly what the fixed-point argument needs.

label: Lipschitz Conditions
notes: Continuity of the right-hand side gives existence but not uniqueness. The extra ingredient is a Lipschitz estimate in the space variable, which smooth fields satisfy locally by the mean value inequality. I stress that Lipschitz control is what prevents two solutions from separating after they touch.

label: Picard Iteration
notes: Picard iteration builds the solution by repeatedly applying the integral operator to an initial guess. On a short interval the operator is a contraction, so the iterates form a Cauchy sequence converging uniformly. This is the constructive heart of the proof, and the successive approximations are computable.

label: Existence and Uniqueness Theorem
notes: This is the fundamental theorem, Picard and Lindelof. On the integral operator the contraction mapping principle delivers a unique fixed point on a small interval around the start time. Smooth right-hand sides are locally Lipschitz, so every smooth vector field has unique integral curves.

label: Maximal Interval of Existence
notes: Local solutions glue into a single maximal solution defined on an open interval. The escape lemma is the key continuation fact: if the maximal interval is bounded above, the solution must eventually leave every compact set. The example x prime equals x squared shows finite-time blow-up concretely.

label: Smooth Dependence on Initial Data
notes: This is the theorem that makes flows smooth. The solution depends smoothly jointly on time and on the initial point and parameters. I emphasize the distinction from each solution being smooth in time alone; here the whole solution map is smooth, which is far stronger and harder.

label: The Variational Equation
notes: Differentiating the flow with respect to its initial condition gives a linear ODE, the variational equation, driven by the Jacobian of the field along the solution. This makes smooth dependence checkable: the sensitivity solves a concrete linear system, illustrated here with the logistic flow map.

label: Linear Systems and the Matrix Exponential
notes: Constant-coefficient linear systems are solved globally by the matrix exponential. For two by two real matrices the trace and determinant classify the phase portrait into saddles, nodes, spirals, and centers. This is the compact laboratory where eigenvalues, exponentials, and pictures all agree.

label: From ODEs to Flows: Recap
notes: We close by tying the analysis back to manifolds. Existence and uniqueness give integral curves, maximal intervals give the flow domain, and smooth dependence makes the flow a smooth map. The partial group law holds wherever every term is defined. These four facts launch the chapter on flows.
